How to Play Sky Team: Rules and Landing

2026-10-26

How to play Sky Team: two players, four dice each, seven rounds, one landing. The pilot takes the blue dice and the co-pilot takes the orange. You talk freely before the roll, then you go quiet and place one die at a time on a cockpit panel. The plane starts at 6,000 feet over Montreal and drops 1,000 feet every round no matter what you do. You land only if the gear and flaps are all green, the axis is level, the approach is clear, and your final speed is slower than your brakes.

My first four attempts ended in a crash. Two spins, one collision, and one landing that was perfect except the plane was still tilted when the wheels touched. My co-pilot was my wife, and after the fourth crash she asked if we could play something less stressful.

Then we landed Montreal. Then Quebec City. Then Rio, which took six tries.

I have around 30 flights in now, on a shelf holding 40+ games, and I can teach the whole thing in 12 minutes. The rules are not the hard part. The hard part is that you cannot say a single number once the dice are out. Every die you place is a sentence your partner has to read, and misreading it is how most landings fail.

What Is in the Box

One control panel with 10 spring switches, 4 blue dice for the pilot, 4 orange dice for the co-pilot, and two cardboard screens so neither of you can see the other's roll. One airplane axis disc, an altitude track with 7 spaces, and 20 airport approach tracks. That is 20 different runways, Montreal first, and every one of them changes the shape of the approach.

You also get 12 little airplane tokens for air traffic, 3 coffee tokens, 2 reroll tokens, a brake marker, and two aerodynamics markers. It is sold as 12 and up, and 10 works for a kid who is happy to be told what to place.

Two things to know before you buy. It plays with exactly two people, no more, no solo variant. And the base box is a complete game, though it is no longer the end of the road: the Turbulence expansion (Kosmos, 2025) adds 20 scenarios and 10 airports, with modules for turbulence, low visibility, and alarms. Buy the base game first. The 20 airports in the box will outlast most couples, and the expansion assumes you can already land Montreal without talking.

Setup: Montreal, 6,000 Feet

Put the control panel between you, both of you on the same side of the table. That placement matters, because you will both be leaning over the same board trying to read it. Slide the altitude track in until 6,000 shows in the screen. Slide the Montreal approach track in until the airport icon shows in the position screen.

Set all 10 switches to green. Put the blue aerodynamics marker between the 4 and the 5 on the speed gauge, and the orange marker between the 8 and the 9. Put the brake marker just left of the 2 on the brake track. Place a reroll token on each reroll icon on the altitude track, which gives you two of them for the flight.

The altitude track has 7 spaces, and that is the whole clock. Seven rounds, 1,000 feet per round, 6,000 to zero. Nothing you roll can change that. Hold onto it, because it reframes the rest of the game.

A Round Is Three Steps

1. Brief. Talk as much as you want about the board. Where the traffic is, whether you want to advance 0, 1, or 2 spaces this round, which light you want to switch on. What you cannot do is talk about the dice, so no "if you roll a 6, put it here" and no asking your partner to use their weakest die. You are talking about the plan, not the roll.

2. Roll and go silent. Roll your four dice behind your screen. From that moment you cannot speak until all eight dice are placed, apart from pointing out a rules mistake. The arrow in the altitude screen decides who places first.

3. Place one die per turn. Each turn you put a single die on a free space. Blue spaces are pilot only, orange spaces are co-pilot only, and a few spaces are both. Many spaces also limit the number, so the first flap switch only accepts a 1 or a 2. You cannot take a die back.

At the end of the round the altitude track advances one space, you take your dice back, and you get to speak again.

The Axis: The Two Dice That Kill You

Every round, both of you must place one die on the axis. This is mandatory, and so is the engines space. If either is missing at the end of a round, you lose immediately.

As soon as the second axis die lands, compare the two numbers. Equal numbers and nothing happens. Different numbers and the airplane disc turns by the difference, toward whoever played higher. A 5 against a 3 turns the plane 2 marks.

Here is the part beginners miss: the tilt does not reset at the end of the round. It carries. Two marks this round plus one mark next round is 3 marks off level, and you need it back to level by the final round to land. If the arrow reaches the spin symbol on either side, you go into a spin and lose on the spot.

Here is why that matters. Axis is the safest place to dump a die, because almost any number works there, and it is also the last place you should wait. If you both hold your axis die until your fourth turn, the last two dice decide whether you crash, and you will have no control left. My first two crashes were exactly that.

Engines: The Only Way to Move

Both of you also place one die on the engines. Add those two numbers together, and that total is your speed for the round.

Pay attention to this number: the two markers on the speed gauge start between 4 and 5 and between 8 and 9. So at the start of the flight a speed of 4 or less moves you 0 spaces on the approach track, a speed of 5 to 8 moves you 1 space, and a speed of 9 or more moves you 2 spaces.

The approach track is where the airport lives and where the traffic sits. If you have to advance and there is an airplane token in your current position, you collide and lose. If the airport icon is in your current position and you have to advance, you overshoot and lose. Both of those are the same message: moving is not free.

Landing Gear and Flaps: Two Different Brakes

Landing gear is pilot only. Three switches, each stamped with two possible numbers, and you can deploy them in any order you like. Switching one on immediately pushes the blue marker one space, which is the marker that decides whether low speed moves you. All three must be green at the end of the game.

Flaps are co-pilot only. Three switches, and these must go in order from top to bottom: 1 or 2 first, then 2 or 3, then 3 or 4. Each flap pushes the orange marker one space, which is the marker that decides whether high speed moves you. All three must be green as well.

This is the quiet engine of the whole game. Gear eats your ability to stop moving slowly. Flaps eat your ability to charge ahead quickly. Deploy both and the plane becomes an object that always creeps forward one space per round, whether you want it or not, because with the blue marker sitting between 7 and 8 and the orange marker past 12, the only sums that move you 0 are 7 or lower.

Radio and Coffee

Radio clears traffic. The pilot has one radio space, the co-pilot has two. The number on the die tells you which space ahead of you gets cleared: a 1 removes the plane in your current position, a 2 removes it from one space ahead, a 3 from two spaces ahead, and so on. If that space is empty, the die is wasted.

Concentration takes any die of any value from either player and pays you a coffee token. Coffee is the only way to bend a die. Spend one token to add or subtract 1 from a die as you place it, capped between 1 and 6, and a 1 cannot wrap around to a 6. You can hold 3 tokens, they carry between rounds, and either player can spend them. Banking a coffee in round two has saved more landings for me than any clever axis play.

Brakes and the Final Round

Brakes are pilot only, and they deploy in order: 2 first, then 4, then 6. Each one pushes the red brake marker forward one step. You do not have to deploy all three, but you cannot stop the plane with fewer than the first one, so plan on at least the 2.

The final round starts when the airport icon is in your current position and the airplane icon is in your current altitude screen. That is the round where the engines flip jobs. Instead of comparing your engine total to the aerodynamics markers, you compare it to your brake marker. Your speed has to be lower than your brakes, or you run off the end of the runway.

You win at the end of that round only if all four things are true: no airplane tokens left on the approach, all gear and flaps switches green, the axis exactly level, and your speed under your brakes. Three out of four is a crash with good paperwork.

This Is Where It Gets Interesting

I thought I was managing altitude for my first ten flights. I was not. The altitude track drops itself, 1,000 feet per round, seven times, and then you are on the ground whether you are ready or not. The descent is not a resource you spend. It is a countdown.

Which means your eight dice a round are never about going down. They are about two things only: horizontal position on the approach track, and the tilt of the plane. Landing is a timing puzzle wearing an aviation costume. The airport has to arrive in your current position in the same round that the plane reaches zero altitude, and if you get there early you fly in circles burning rounds you do not have.

That is also why the gear and flaps are so expensive. Each one is a die you did not spend on radio or speed, and each one narrows the number range that lets you hold position. The first time you deploy all six, the table gets very quiet, because you have just committed to moving forward every round until touchdown.

The Four Ways I Crashed

I saved the axis for last. Round three, two dice left, a 1 and a 6, both of us holding. Difference of 5 turns the plane into the spin symbol. That one took four seconds.

I advanced into traffic. Speed of 9, plane token sitting in the next space, and no radio die left to clear it. Collision. The rulebook is polite about it. You are simply dead.

I landed with the gear up. Everything looked calm. Traffic cleared, axis level, brakes set. Two gear lights still red because I had spent those dice on radio early. That is not a landing.

I came in too hot. Speed 9 with the brake marker sitting between 4 and 5. The wheels touched and the plane kept going into whatever is past the runway. My wife still brings that one up.

Which Co-op Should You Buy

So now you know the machine. The question is whether this is the right two-player co-op for your table, because there are three good answers and they cost very different amounts.

GamePlayersTimeFeelPrice I found
Sky Team2 only20 minSilent, tense, mission ladder$32.99
The Crew2-520 minTrick taking, campaign of 50 missions$14.95
Pandemic2-445 minBigger board, longer arc, more rules$49.99

Sky Team is the one I reach for when there are exactly two of us and we want 20 minutes with our brains on. It was $32.99 on Amazon the week I checked, with a $30.63 offer from other sellers. It won the Spiel des Jahres in 2024, and it was the first game built strictly for two players to take that award, which surprised a lot of people who assumed the prize was reserved for family games.

If your group is often more than two, get The Crew instead. It is $14.95, it plays 2 to 5, and 50 missions for that price is the best value in my collection. It scratches a similar itch, except the silence rule is built into trick taking and you can bring friends.

Pandemic at $49.99 is the wrong first co-op for most couples. It is good, it is also 45 minutes and a lot of rule explaining, and one player usually ends up quarterbacking the table. Sky Team avoids that problem by design, because you literally cannot tell your partner what to do.

Full stats for the game live on my Sky Team page, and the wider field is on the cooperative games list.

The Shelf Test

Here is the Shelf Test. Would this survive 10 plays on a shelf that already holds 40 boxes? Ten plays is about three hours of Sky Team, and you will not have finished the green airports by then. Twenty airports, four difficulty colors, and modifiers like wind and kerosene that change the arithmetic, so the box keeps handing you a new runway instead of asking you to replay the same one.

The honest flaw is the player count. Two means two. If your regular game night is four people, half the table sits out, and no house rule fixes that without breaking the silence that makes the game work. There is also no talking variant in the box. Loosen that rule and the puzzle dissolves, because the whole challenge is reading a partner who cannot speak. Buy this for a partner, a roommate, or a friend you see one on one, not for a group.

If you need something that handles a bigger table, my cooperative list has the ones that scale, and the two player list covers what to play when you want a fight instead of a partnership. New to the hobby entirely? Start with the beginner list before you buy a cockpit.

Here is the part that matters. Learn the axis first, spend coffee early, and treat the gear and flaps like the brakes they secretly are. Sky Team was $32.99 when I last checked, list price sits near $35, so anything under $31 is a solid deal and $30.63 has shown up from third party sellers. Let my wallet take the hit on a black difficulty airport instead of yours.
